how-should-a-consignment-shop-mark-down..text:
Consignment Markdown Planner · guide

How should a consignment shop mark down? 30/60/90-day schedule math

Short answer: mark an item down when the extra chance of selling it this week is worth more than the cut you give up and the shelf week you save. A fixed schedule gets close; working it per item gets closer, and also tells you which items were never worth the slot.

A worked example

A designer silk blazer is tagged at $120. It sells about 8% of weeks at full price, you keep 40% of the sale, a rack slot costs $0.60 a week, handling is $2, and the item stays 12 weeks. Each 10% off lifts the weekly sell chance by 35% of its base rate.

  • Never marking down: the blazer sells 63% of the time and nets the shop $23.61.
  • A fixed 25% off at week 5 and 50% off at week 9: $25.45.
  • The best schedule, 10% off from week 1, 25% off in weeks 8-11 and 40% off in week 12: $26.76, selling 81% of the time, with the consignor paid about $49.23 on average.

The gain per item is small; across a floor of hundreds of items it is the difference between a rack that turns and one that fills with last season.

Which items to decline

A $12 graphic tee that sells 10% of weeks, with a 40% shop share and the same $0.60 slot, nets -$1.63 even on its best schedule (25% off from week 1, 40% off from week 6). It would only pay at a price of about $17.93 or a shop share near 59.8%. Tell consignors that items under that price are not accepted, or take them at a higher split.

What to feed it

  1. Weekly sell rate from your own history: items of that kind sold per week they were on the floor.
  2. Shelf cost per week: rent and floor staff time for the area, divided by item slots.
  3. Lift: compare sell-through in the weeks before and after your last markdowns.

Check the consignment agreement first: some promise consignors a markdown schedule or price floor, and those terms come before any optimum.

Questions

How long should a consignment shop wait before marking an item down?

There is no fixed answer; it depends on how fast items like it sell and what a week of shelf space costs you. Items that sell quickly at full price can hold their tag longer. Items on a costly slot or with a slow sell rate pay to start marking down early. The planner finds the best start week for each item from your own numbers.

Is a 30/60/90-day markdown schedule good enough?

It is a sensible default and rarely a disaster, but it treats every item the same. The planner compares it with the best schedule for each item and prints the dollars the fixed rule leaves behind.

Which items should a consignment shop refuse?

Items whose expected shop cut, over the weeks they are likely to sit, does not cover shelf space and handling. Low-ticket items on a costly shelf are the usual losers. The planner names the price or shop share at which each declined item would pay.

The worked example is illustrative arithmetic, not a forecast of what will sell.

CONSIGNMENT MARKDOWN PLANNER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

When should a consignment shop mark things down, and what should it decline?

Every week an item sits, it uses a rack slot you pay for. A fixed rule (25% off at 30 days, 50% at 60) treats a $12 tee and a $210 handbag the same. Paste your items — price, how fast it sells, your share of the sale and what a slot costs per week — and get the exact markdown schedule with the highest expected profit for each, which items are not worth taking in, and what a fixed rule leaves on the table.

For consignment and resale boutiques, thrift, vintage and furniture shops. Nothing is uploaded: the text box is analysed in this browser and never leaves your device.

    Prefer a CLI?

    Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

    node cli.mjs plan items.csv --weeks 12 --lift 0.35 --levels 0,10,25,40,50 --json
cat items.csv | node cli.mjs plan - --handling 2

    Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. More: How should a consignment shop mark down? 30/60/90-day schedule math.

    What's recognised

    InputHandling

    The schedule is exact for the numbers you type (dynamic programming over every non-decreasing schedule, up to 200 items). Seasonality, consignor price-floor agreements, items that sell as a group and unsold-item returns or donation value are not modelled; enter shelf cost and sell rates as they really are for you.

    Common questions

    Does it upload my item list?

    No. The browser page works on the text you paste, in your own browser, and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

    How is the best schedule found?

    Each week an item can sell with a chance that rises with the discount, and every week on the floor costs shelf space. The tool works backwards week by week over the markdown levels you allow, never raising a price, and keeps the schedule with the highest expected net to the shop. It is checked against trying every possible schedule in the tests.

    Why would it tell me to decline an item?

    If the shop's cut of the likely sale does not cover shelf space and handling, taking the item loses money even at the best schedule. The tool says what price or shop share would make the item worth taking.

    Where do the sell rates and the lift come from?

    From your own history: how many weeks items like this usually sit, and how much faster they sell after a markdown. They are your estimates, so treat the plan as a decision aid, not a forecast.

    Who is it for?

    Consignment and resale boutiques, thrift and vintage shops and furniture consignors deciding when to mark things down and what to accept.
